points.label: Loss measures prediction error
points.description: The learner states that a loss function takes a model's prediction and the true label and returns a number quantifying how wrong the prediction is, with lower values meaning better predictions and (typically) zero meaning a perfect prediction.

points.label: Loss defines the training objective
points.description: The learner explains that training is framed as minimizing the loss averaged (or summed) over the training examples, so the loss function is what turns 'learning' into a concrete optimization problem: the model's parameters are adjusted specifically to push this number down.

points.label: Different tasks use different losses
points.description: The learner names or describes at least one concrete loss and matches it to its task type: e.g. mean squared error (average of squared differences) for regression, or cross-entropy / log loss (penalizing confident wrong class probabilities) for classification, and says why that pairing makes sense.

points.label: Loss guides the direction of updates
points.description: The learner explains the feedback role of the loss: because the loss depends on the parameters, its gradient (or more informally, how the loss changes when a parameter changes) tells the training algorithm which direction to adjust each parameter, which is why the loss should be differentiable or at least give usable feedback.

points.label: Loss is not the same as the evaluation metric
points.description: The learner distinguishes the loss optimized during training from human-facing evaluation metrics like accuracy: e.g. accuracy is a step function that gives no gradient signal, so models train on a surrogate like cross-entropy while being reported on accuracy, and a lower loss does not always mean a better metric score.

misconceptions.summary: The loss function is the same thing as accuracy — they are just two words for the model's score.
misconceptions.belief: I take loss and accuracy to be two names for the same score of how well the model is doing — loss counts it as wrongness and accuracy counts it as rightness, but it's one measurement.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Both numbers move together in most training curves and both describe how good the model is, so they look like the same quantity expressed two ways.
misconceptions.fallback_line: Loss going down and accuracy going up are the same score flipped around — two words for one measurement — so we might as well train the model to maximize accuracy directly.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that accuracy only counts right vs wrong and changes in jumps, giving no smooth signal to learn from, while a loss like cross-entropy varies continuously with the model's confidence; that is why training minimizes a loss rather than directly maximizing accuracy, and why the two can move differently.

misconceptions.summary: There is one universal loss function that every model uses.
misconceptions.belief: I assume there's one standard loss formula that all models share — an error is just the gap between prediction and truth, so mean squared error should work for any task, including classification.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Every loss ultimately measures prediction error, so it seems like one general-purpose formula for 'how far off you were' should cover every problem.
misconceptions.fallback_line: An error is just the gap between the prediction and the truth, so one formula like squared error should work for every kind of model, classification included — that's the whole point of it.
misconceptions.correction: The learner clarifies that the loss is a design choice matched to the task and goals: regression commonly uses squared error, classification commonly uses cross-entropy, and the choice changes what errors the model cares about (e.g. squared error punishes large errors disproportionately), so choosing the loss is part of defining the problem.

misconceptions.summary: If the training loss reaches (near) zero, the model is finished and will perform perfectly in the real world.
misconceptions.belief: If my training loss gets to nearly zero, the model has learned the problem completely, so it should perform just as well on any new data it sees.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Zero loss literally means zero error on everything the model was graded on, which sounds like the definition of having fully learned the task.
misconceptions.fallback_line: My training loss is basically zero, so the model makes no mistakes anymore — it's done learning and it'll work just as well on any new data it sees.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that near-zero training loss only means the model fits the training examples, which may indicate memorization/overfitting; what matters is the loss or metric on held-out data, and a gap between low training loss and high validation loss is a warning sign, not a success.

beginner: So the loss is just one number? How can one number describe how wrong the model is across thousands of examples?
What happens to the loss when the model makes a perfect prediction? And a terrible one?
Why do we need a formula for wrongness at all — couldn't the model just count how many answers it got right?
confident: Loss and accuracy are the same thing, so I can just train the model to maximize accuracy directly.
Mean squared error works for every problem — I'd use it for classification too, since an error is an error.
My training loss hit almost zero, so the model is done and guaranteed to work great on new data.
skeptic: The loss is something a human chose. If I picked a different loss I'd get a different model — so isn't 'the best model' just an artifact of that arbitrary choice?
Squared error punishes one big mistake more than many small ones. Who says that's the right trade-off — what if in my application ten small errors are worse than one big one?
If models train on a surrogate loss instead of the metric we actually care about, aren't we always optimizing the wrong thing and just hoping it correlates?
